content:
The image shows a corn ear with the husk partially pulled back, revealing a mass of dark black, powdery/sooty material completely replacing the kernels. The ear is heavily blackened with what appears to be a mass of dark fungal spores. The surrounding husk tissue is tan/brown and dried.

Key features:
- Affected part: corn ear
- Color: dense black, powdery mass covering the entire ear
- Texture: sooty/dusty appearance, replacing kernel tissue
- Husk is intact but peeled back revealing the black mass

This is a classic presentation of **Common Smut** (*Ustilago maydis*) — which produces large, black, sooty galls filled with teliospores on corn ears, turning the entire ear into a black spore mass. Head Smut affects the tassel/head region. Common Smut commonly affects ears and produces exactly this appearance: dark black, powdery masses replacing kernel tissue within the husk.
